title: Scipio's small bath
hook: Seneca visits Scipio's plain country house and its tiny dark bath (Letters 86)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was apes, the bees: gather widely, digest, and make one honey. Your line was one sound rises.

Scipio Africanus was the Roman general who beat Hannibal, the man Seneca calls the terror of Carthage. After all of it, he left Rome for a farm at Liternum, on the coast. Long afterward, Seneca goes there and stays in Scipio's own house. He looks over the stone walls and the towers, and then he finds the bath. It's tiny, and dark, and he's delighted. The eighty-sixth letter is a tour, and a little sermon on plumbing.
screen: `THE GENERAL WHO BEAT HANNIBAL.` → `A FARM AT LITERNUM.` → `A BATH, TINY AND DARK.`

segments.voice: The house is built of squared stone, with a wall around a wood and towers at both ends. Seneca writes lying in the very house of Scipio, and he has paid his respects at what people say is Scipio's tomb. Then the bath: small, narrow and dark, in the old style. The old Romans, Seneca says, didn't think a bath was warm unless it was dim. Here the man who terrified Carthage washed a body tired from farm work, under this cheap roof, on this plain floor. Now, Seneca says, people feel poor unless their walls shine with big precious mirrors, unless their pools are lined with marble, unless water pours from silver taps. In Scipio's bath there were slits rather than windows. Now people sneer at any bath that doesn't take in the sun all day through huge windows. Seneca isn't telling anyone to bathe in the dark. His point is that the great man of Rome needed very little, and lost nothing by it. Looking back on the week, from Attalus's old wine and school in old age to the stage kings, the honest timetable and the bees, the thread is plainness: honest memory, honest days, honest pleasure.
screen: `SCIPIO'S HOUSE AT LITERNUM.` · `A SMALL, DARK BATH.` · `NOW EVERYONE WANTS MIRRORS.` · `THE GREAT MAN NEEDED LITTLE.` · then, large: `PLAIN WAS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Choose one plain thing near you, a glass of water, a slice of bread, the light through a window, and give it your full attention, as if it were a hero's bath: its texture, its weight, its use. Let it be enough for this minute, and if a wish for something fancier rises, let it pass.
Balneolum. Latin for a little bath: Scipio Africanus washed in one, narrow and dark, after farm work, and Seneca says it was enough. Today's word.
Your line: plain was enough. Next week, Seneca on learning and on living together. That's a week of Seneca.

howItsDone: Some people inspired by Seneca keep one part of their life deliberately plain, a meal, a room or a routine, and take pleasure in it rather than in upgrades.

original.note: Latin: a little bath. Seneca, Letters 86.4, describes Scipio's as narrow and dark in the old style.

what a scholar hears: Letters 86.1–13; Scipio Africanus (died c. 183 BCE) retired to Liternum; Seneca also tells of planting olive trees there with the farmer Aegialus (86.14–21).

chat.says: Why did Seneca get so excited about an old, tiny bath?
options: Scipio, the hero who beat Hannibal, washed in a small dark one; plain was enough for him.
Seneca loved old buildings and wanted Rome's baths restored to their glory.
Seneca thought dark baths were healthier, so he told everyone to use one.
chat.meaning: Letter eighty-six: the general who terrified Carthage washed in a small, dark bath. Seneca's point is that the great man needed very little.

Scipio Africanus.meaning: the Roman general who defeated Hannibal

Carthage.meaning: a North African city, Rome's great rival

Liternum.meaning: the coastal place where Scipio had his farm

notes: Letters 86.1: Seneca writes lying in Scipio's villa, having visited his tomb (or the altar people take for his tomb). 86.4: the house of squared stone, walls around a wood, towers; 'balneolum angustum, tenebricosum ex consuetudine antiqua'. 86.5: Scipio washing a body tired from farm work. 86.6–8: contemporary luxury (mirrors, marble, silver taps); 86.8: such baths now called caves ('cavernas'). Confirm details.
'Some two and a half centuries later': Scipio died c. 183 BCE; Letters 86 c. 64 CE, about 245 years. Confirm.

The week look-back wrongly included day 469 (last week) and skipped 472–473; corrected. 'Beat Hannibal' is standard history, not stated in Letter 86; Seneca's own phrase is 'horror Carthaginis' (86.5).
